```{r}
#Part A

#Question 1

Respondent<- 1:20
Sex<-c(2,2,1,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,1,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,1,2)
FathersOccupation<-c(1,3,3,3,1,2,3,1,1,1,3,2,1,3,3,1,3,1,2,1)
PersonsAtHome<-c(5,7,3,8,5,9,6,7,8,4,7,5,4,7,8,8,3,11,7,6)
SiblingsAtSchool<-c(6,4,4,1,2,1,5,3,1,2,3,2,5,5,2,1,2,5,3,2)
TypesOfHouses<-c(1,2,3,1,1,3,3,1,2,3,2,3,2,2,3,3,3,3,3,2)

length(Respondent)
length(Sex)
length(FathersOccupation)
length(PersonsAtHome)
length(SiblingsAtSchool)
length(TypesOfHouses)

survey<-data.frame(Respondent, Sex, FathersOccupation,
                     PersonsAtHome, SiblingsAtSchool, TypesOfHouses)
print(survey)

#Question A1A
str(survey)
summary(survey)

#Question A1B
dim(survey)
nrow(survey)
ncol(survey)

#Question A1C
survey$Sex<-factor(survey$Sex,levels = c(1, 2),labels = c("Male", "Female"))

survey$FathersOccupation<-factor(survey$FathersOccupation,levels = c(1, 2, 3),labels = c("Farmer", "Driver", "Others"))

survey$TypesOfHouses<-factor(survey$TypesOfHouses,levels = c(1, 2, 3),labels = c("Wood", "Semi-Concrete", "Concrete"))

str(survey)

#Question A1D
mean(survey$Respondent)
mean(survey$PersonsAtHome)
mean(survey$SiblingsAtSchool)

#Question A1E
survey[1:5, ]

#Question A1F
types_houses <- survey$TypesOfHouses
types_houses

#Question A1G
survey[survey$Sex == "Male" & survey$FathersOccupation == "Farmer", ]

#Question A1H
survey[survey$Sex == "Female" & survey$SiblingsAtSchool >= 5, ]

#Question A2
#In survey data, every row represents one specific respondent, so each column must have exactly one value per person.

#Question A3
#Sex, FathersOccupation, and TypesOfHouses are nominal categories represented by numbers. PersonsAtHome and SiblingsAtSchool are actual counts. Treating Sex as a quantity is misleading because the numbers 1 and 2 are just labels with no numeric meaning.

#Question A4
#Someone unfamiliar with the legend would see a column of 1s and 2s and have no idea what they represent. They might assume 1 means a low score or a first group without any context.

#Question A5
nrow(survey[survey$Sex == "Male", ])
sum(survey$Sex == "Male")
#Only 3 out of 20 respondents are male. This very small sample size means any pattern observed among males, such as a common occupation or house type, could easily be a coincidence rather than a real trend.

#Question A6
#R stores data as numbers unless explicitly told otherwise. It has no way of knowing that the values 1, 2, and 3 in Sex represent categories rather than quantities, because the distinction exists only in the researcher’s understanding, not in the data itself.

#Question A7
#The mean of PersonsAtHome at 6.65 is meaningful because it represents an actual average count of people living in a household, which is a real and interpretable quantity. The mean of Sex at 1.85 is not meaningful because sex is a category encoded as 1 and 2, and the average of those codes has no real-world interpretation.
```
